transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30 16:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Evan (Redwood SE), Liam (Pegasus Head of Platform), Rita (Pegasus SecOps), Omar (Pegasus SRE), Sofia (Pegasus Cloud Arch)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to understand Pegasus' private connectivity constraints and preferred topology for Redwood Private. Main questions: transit-gateway vs VPC peering, private endpoints, region constraints for residency, and egress handling.

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan with Redwood, AE on this account. We brought Priya and Evan from our solutions team to cover network patterns. Could you quick intro yourselves?
00:12 Liam: Sure yeah Liam Chen, head of platform at Pegasus. We run a multi-region infra, mostly us-west-2 and eu-west-1; we'll be expanding to ap-southeast later this year.
00:20 Rita: Rita Morales, SecOps. I'm here for the security questions — SOC2, encryption, KMS, that sort of thing.
00:27 Omar: Omar Patel, SRE, I'll be responsible for connectivity and testing.
00:31 Sofia: Sofia, cloud architect, focusing on network topology.
00:34 Priya: Thanks all. Quick agenda: current infra, target traffic patterns, what constraints you have for private deployments, and then go over options — transit gateway, peering, private endpoints, and egress requirements.
00:46 Liam: Sounds good. We are evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. For production, compliance wants private only — VPC connectivity into Redwood control plane that doesn't cross the public internet. We also need audit logging retained for 2 years, and KMS-managed encryption keys.
01:02 Jordan: Totally, that's pretty common. Can you talk about scale — token volume and concurrency? That will affect topology recommendations.
01:09 Liam: Roughly 5 to 10 million tokens a day, peak concurrency around 60 qps for generation endpoints, and a few hundred qps for embeddings across microservices. Latency target sub-200ms p50 for short prompts.
01:23 Priya: Helpful. For that volume, we usually recommend a Dedicated pool for predictable throughput. For Private the networking options are mostly: 1) VPC peering to a Redwood VPC per-region, 2) Transit gateway based hub-and-spoke for multi-region connectivity, or 3) Private endpoints (interface endpoints) with egress NAT allowed. Each has tradeoffs.
01:44 Omar: Can you explain the difference in egress patterns? Our compliance team will not allow egress to public IPs from the VPC unless it's through our proxy.
01:51 Evan: Sure. With VPC peering traffic is entirely private — it's routed via the peering link and doesn't traverse the public internet. With Transit Gateway you get a single hub that can connect multiple customer VPCs and Redwood's VPCs, which simplifies routing and centralizes firewall controls. Private endpoints (like interface endpoints) can also be used; they create ENIs in your VPC that resolve to Redwood's service. The difference is operational: peering is direct and simple but scales poorly at large fan-out; transit gateway is better for many spokes.
02:20 Rita: If we use interface endpoints, do you require inbound rules? Our security team is worried about service-initiated traffic.
02:28 Priya: Redwood will only initiate responses to established connections from your VPC. The flow is customer-originated TLS to the service endpoint. No autonomous inbound init from our side. There are occasional control plane callbacks for metrics but those can be routed over the private control plane or via a secure webhook if needed.
02:46 Sofia: We have Shared Services VPC with centralized egress through NAT GW and a proxy. If Redwood needs to call back for telemetry, can that go through our proxy?
02:55 Jordan: Yes, we can route callbacks through your egress. We typically support a private control plane option for Private customers so telemetry and control plane traffic can be contained inside the customer's network boundary when required. We'll detail in the security pack.
03:08 Liam: Regions: our EU workloads must remain in eu-west-1 and cannot egress to us-west-2. Can Redwood provide per-region private endpoints so inference happens in-region?
03:18 Priya: Absolutely. For Private we can provision region-specific endpoints and keep inference in-region. We'll provision dedicated nodes in the region(s) you choose. We also support model pinning so requests to eu endpoints use eu-hosted model variants.
03:32 Omar: For peering, we have strict CIDR usage. What about overlapping ranges?
03:37 Evan: CIDR overlap is a blocker for peering. Transit gateway gives more flexibility if you use NATing or route translation, but it's more complex. Another pattern is to stand up a small transit VPC with unique CIDRs used only for peering to Redwood.
03:53 Rita: What about authentication? SSO? SAML? Service accounts?
03:57 Jordan: We support SAML SSO for the Redwood console and RBAC. For service-to-service we use mTLS and API keys, and in Private we can integrate with your KMS for key wrapping or bring-your-own-keys for at-rest keys. We'll send the SSO and KMS docs.
04:13 Sofia: Any specific firewall ports we need to open for peering or endpoints?
04:18 Priya: For interface endpoints, it's standard TLS on 443 to the endpoint ENIs. For peering, there are no ports to open — routing handles it. If you use transit gateway, you'll need to allow the same but control plane callbacks might use separate ports; we'll include a port breakdown in the network diagram.
04:36 Omar: Can you run benchmarks from within our VPC? We want end-to-end latency numbers not just from public cloud.
04:42 Priya: Yes. We can arrange a pilot where we provision a Dedicated instance in your region, and run synthetic requests from your VPC through the chosen topology — peering or transit — and measure latency / throughput. That typically takes a day to set up once we have CIDRs and an account owner.
04:56 Liam: How do you handle KV cache and batching across zones? We use long-lived sessions and want ACKs for cache warm-up.
05:05 Evan: Our runtime supports KV cache affinity per instance. For Private deployments we can pin caches to instances within the same AZ to avoid cross-AZ egress. Batching is handled at the inference layer and we expose knobs for max batching latency; we'll share recommended settings.
05:20 Rita: Audit logs — retention of two years — is that included or an add-on?
05:25 Jordan: Two-year audit retention is part of our enterprise package (private). We can also deliver logs to your S3/GCS bucket via secured log export or push to a SIEM via a private delivery method. We'll include options and costs.
05:37 Sofia: Cost question: what's the rough delta between Dedicated in-region vs Private-hosted in our VPC?
05:44 Jordan: Ballpark: Dedicated (Redwood-managed) is usually cheaper because we amortize across customers, but it requires trusting Redwood-managed network egress. Private in-customer-VPC has higher fixed network and ops cost, plus data egress considerations. We'll put together a TCO sheet with options: Hosted, Dedicated, Private with transit gateway, Private with peering.
06:05 Omar: Any compliance blockers for on-prem air-gapped? We might need an air-gapped option for some customers.
06:11 Priya: We do have an on-prem/offline packaging option but it involves more integration and longer lead time—typically a multi-month engagement. Fine for regulated customers but not ideal for PD-0 rapid pilots.
06:23 Liam: Ok next, very practical — what do you need from us to start a pilot?
06:28 Jordan: Three things: CIDR ranges for the VPC(s) you want to connect, a technical contact for firewall/proxy config (looks like Omar), and a list of regions and expected peak QPS per region. Also PO for pilot if needed.
06:40 Liam: We'll get that to you.
06:42 Rita: Anything in the way of data residency? We need contractual language that data processed in eu remains in eu.
06:47 Jordan: We'll include model pinning and region residency clauses and can restrict replication. We'll attach that to the legal/contract pack.
06:55 Evan: Quick note on DNS: interface endpoints will require you to update private hosted zones or route 53 resolver rules so services resolve to the endpoint IPs. We'll provide a step-by-step.
07:08 Priya: I'll follow up with two diagrams:
- Option A: Direct VPC peering per region — simple routing, minimal components, works if CIDRs don't overlap.
- Option B: Central transit-gateway — better for many spokes and centralized egress via proxy. Includes note on cost per attachment and potential throughput limits.
07:25 Sofia: Does Redwood support bringing our HSM for key wrapping?
07:29 Jordan: Yes, we support KMS integrations and some HSM key wrapping options. Priya will include supported providers and the integration flow.
07:38 Liam: Great. Recap next steps?
07:41 Jordan: Recap: we (Redwood) will send SOC2/SAML/KMS docs, network diagrams for two options, port list, and a TCO comparison. Pegasus will send CIDR, regions, and designate Omar as network lead. We'll schedule a 30-min pilot planning call next week.
07:58 Rita: Sounds good.
08:00 Jordan: Anything else?
08:02 Omar: One small thing — can Redwood support egress to a proxy with authentication headers so our proxy can do token-based allowlist?
08:09 Evan: Yes, we can configure callbacks to use a customer proxy with header injection for auth. We'll document the exact header scheme.
08:17 Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite for the pilot planning.

End of transcript.
